How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Event segmentation divides continuous experience into discrete events. In experiments where changes in context mark event boundaries, pairs of items encoded across an event boundary are typically encoded less accurately and judged as further apart in time than pairs encoded within the same event. However, how these differences depend on event reminders available at retrieval remains unclear. Four pre-registered experiments combined memory tests with manipulations of event reminders. Memory for event membership supported crossboundary ordering only when event order was also remembered correctly. The usual withinevent order advantage reversed when sequences contained fewer, longer events. Incorrect event reminders reduced order accuracy and reversed the distance effect, making within-event pairs seem farther apart than cross-boundary pairs. These reversals challenge accounts that explain boundary effects solely through segmentation during encoding. We developed and fitted a retrieved-context model that assigns items to remembered events and reconstructs their positions from item-and event-level temporal evidence. The same reconstructed positions support temporal order and distance judgments, allowing the model to capture classic and reversed effects. Taken together, the findings show that the magnitude and direction of event-boundary effects depend on event reminders available or reconstructed at retrieval. Interpreting these behavioural markers as evidence of segmentation during encoding therefore requires accounting for retrieval conditions.

The Contribution of Retrieval Processes to Behavioural Markers of Event Segmentation

Although experience unfolds continuously, people naturally parse it into discrete events (Kurby & Zacks, 2008; Zacks et al., 2007). According to Event Segmentation Theory, people maintain an active representation, or event model, of the current situation in order to predict what will happen next (Zacks et al., 2007). When incoming information violates these predictions, the event model can be updated, giving rise to event boundaries that divide continuous experience into meaningful events (Reynolds et al., 2007; Zacks et al., 2011). The process of segmentation is thought to have robust behavioural consequences.

In typical event segmentation paradigms, participants encode sequences of items that are grouped into events (sub-sequences of items) and are assumed to perceive a boundary when they switch from one event to the next. For example, in DuBrow and Davachi's seminal study (2013), participants made judgements about stimuli presented in a long sequence. Events corresponded to short, alternating sub-sequences of objects and faces that they judged as "bigger/smaller" (relative to a shoebox) or "female/male", respectively. At test, participants were presented with pairs of studied items and judged their encoding order. Across such studies, temporal order judgments are typically less accurate for pairs encoded across a boundary than for pairs encoded within one event (DuBrow & Davachi, 2013; Heusser et al., 2018; Horner et al., 2016; Pu et al., 2022; Y. C. Wang & Egner, 2022). Cross-boundary pairs are also commonly judged farther apart in time (Bangert et al., 2020; Clewett et al., 2020).

Several theoretical accounts explain these behavioural effects in terms of representational changes produced by event boundaries during encoding. The Event Horizon Model, for example, proposes that continuous experience is segmented into distinct event models. When these models share features, they can compete during retrieval of a particular event (Radvansky & Zacks, 2017). Context-based models also conceptualise context as a slowly drifting internal state to which items become bound during encoding (Howard et al., 2015; Howard & Kahana, 2002; Lohnas et al., 2015; Polyn et al., 2009). Event boundaries are assumed to produce an abrupt shift in this context, reducing contextual similarity and associative continuity between items encountered across events (Horner et al., 2016; Polyn et al., 2009). Pu et al. (2022) proposed that boundaries not only decrease contextual similarity, but reset temporal context toward its initial state, disrupting its correspondence with serial position and thereby impairing temporal-order memory across events. The contextual dissimilarity produced by a boundary may also explain why cross-boundary pairs are perceived as farther apart in time, as greater representational similarity between experiences is associated with judgments of greater temporal proximity (Ezzyat & Davachi, 2014). Consistent with these accounts, event boundaries produce discontinuities in neural temporal-context representations during encoding (Baldassano et al., 2017; Lohnas et al., 2023).

Retrieved-context models further assume that retrieving an item can reinstate its encoding context, thereby promoting the retrieval of other items associated with similar contexts. Evidence for reactivation of intervening items during order judgments supports a role for retrieved associations in temporal memory (DuBrow & Davachi, 2014). Horner et al. (2016), for example, used contextual similarity to predict which candidate would be selected as the object immediately before or after a probe. The boundary effect arose because objects studied across a spatial boundary were associated with less similar contexts. For judgments involving two probes, the models of Pu et al. (2022) and Peng et al. (2025) compared each probe's context with the context of the first item in the sequence. Greater dissimilarity from this reference provided evidence that an item had occurred later. Lohnas et al. (2023) similarly modelled how disruption of temporal context at boundaries during study shapes contextual reinstatement and the order in which items are freely recalled. Together, these models share an encoding-based explanation of canonical boundary effects: boundaries alter contextual representations during encoding, which subsequently shape temporal memory. Wen and Egner (2022) showed that the source information available at retrieval can alter the direction and magnitude of behavioural boundary effects. Their investigation was motivated by the observation that the classic within-event advantage in temporal order memory can clash with everyday experience. It may not be difficult to remember that a speaker discussed the hippocampus in a lecture theatre before we refilled our water bottle in the kitchenette, a crossboundary judgment, yet we may struggle to recall whether the lecturer discussed the hippocampus before or after the cortex, a within-event judgment. In everyday life, such actions are often embedded in distinctive contexts, making their event sources readily retrievable. Wen and Egner (2022) defined events using orienting tasks and stimulus category change (experiment 1), task change with or without stimulus category changes (experiment 2), or nonrepeating coloured frames that surrounded each item (experiments 3-4). In experiments 1-2, the test items could themselves indicate their encoding contexts. In experiments 3-4, test items were presented with or without their original coloured frames, which served as event reminders.

Reinstating the frames improved cross-boundary order memory and could make it more accurate than within-event order memory, "flipping" the classic effect. Thus, the same encoding procedure produced different behavioural boundary effects depending on the source information available at retrieval. Explaining these results requires specifying how source information available at retrieval can reverse the relative accuracy of within-event and cross-boundary order judgments.

The mechanism through which source information supports temporal order judgments remains unclear. One possibility is that an item's event information acts as a reminder, helping recover when the item occurred. This would extend the benefits of retrieval cues for recovering associated items or experiences (Conway & Bekerian, 1987; Godden & Baddeley, 1975; Tulving & Pearlstone, 1966) to temporal information. For example, remembering the lecture-theatre and kitchenette contexts may help recover when the two corresponding actions occurred, allowing their temporal relation to be reconstructed from item-level evidence. In that case, we may predict that temporal order judgements will be better when participants correctly remember which event each item was associated with (source memory). Surprisingly, in Wen and Egner's source-absent condition, correctly identifying the items' coloured frames on a later source-memory test was not associated with better temporal order memory. Correctly identifying an item's event may be insufficient for cross-boundary judgments if these also depend on remembering event order. For example, remembering that the lecture preceded the visit to the kitchenette could then help determine that discussing the hippocampus occurred before refilling the water bottle. On this account, the contribution of source memory to cross-boundary judgments should depend in addition to source memory on memory for the order of the event reminders (event-order memory).

Source information may also influence temporal-distance judgments. Wen and Egner (2022) found that the difference between cross-boundary and within-event distance ratings was larger when the coloured frames identifying the items' events were shown at test than when they were omitted. In an analysis combining these conditions, distance ratings also varied with how accurately participants later identified the items' frames. Source information might help recover item-level temporal information, or support inferences about separation based on whether items are remembered as belonging to the same or different events. The latter possibility suggests that errors in source retrieval could distort perceived distance even when the studied sequence is held constant.

Taken together, a formal account of these retrieval processes is also currently lacking, and Wen and Egner's results reveal that it is necessary for a fuller account of the memory consequences of event segmentation. A joint account of temporal order and distance judgments needs to explain how remembered event membership and order shape those judgments, including when that information is wrong. Hierarchical accounts of memory provide a basis for this explanation by distinguishing groups and the positions of their contents (Farrell, 2012). We propose that people use this organisation to reconstruct when items occurred. They first infer which event contained an item, then combine evidence about that event's position in the sequence with evidence about the item's position within that event. Misidentifying the event can therefore bring the wrong event's temporal evidence into the reconstruction. The reconstructed positions then identify which item came first and how far apart the items were. For example, items remembered as belonging to different events could be reconstructed far apart even when the order of those events is misremembered. Order and distance judgments can therefore show different effects of errors in event memory even though they draw on the same reconstructed sequence.

We addressed these empirical and theoretical gaps across four preregistered experiments.

Experiment 1 was designed as conceptual replication of Wen and Egner's headline finding, examining whether the availability of event-source information at retrieval alters behavioural boundary effects. Experiment 2 tested whether the benefit of source memory depends on memory for event order. Experiment 3 examined whether the effect of source reinstatement depends on how readily event order can be reconstructed. Finally, Experiment 4 directly manipulated the event structure implied at retrieval to test its causal influence on temporal order and distance judgments. Building on existing context-based accounts, we also developed a new retrieved-context model that separates item-level and event-level temporal evidence and specifies how they are integrated at retrieval. The model formalises how retrieval conditions can change the magnitude and direction of behavioural boundary effects, even when the event structure established during encoding is preserved.

These retrieval effects matter beyond the present experiments because temporal judgments are used as behavioural markers of event segmentation in both fundamental and translational research. Event segmentation has wide-ranging consequences for cognition, supporting narrative comprehension, learning, skill acquisition, and memory (Pettijohn & Radvansky, 2016; Richmond et al., 2017; Speer & Zacks, 2005; Zacks & Swallow, 2007). Indeed, event segmentation ability predicts better subsequent memory (Flores et al., 2017; Sargent et al., 2013), and event segmentation deficits predict maladaptive functioning (Reagh et al., 2020; Wyrobnik et al., 2022a Wyrobnik et al., , 2022b;; Zacks et al., 2016). Interpreting temporal judgments in this broader context requires distinguishing the contribution of the studied event structure from that of event information recovered or supplied at retrieval.

Experiment 1

The research reported here was inspired by the intriguing observations of Wen and Egner (2022), with this first experiment designed as a conceptual replication. They pointed out that in daily life, the encoding context of each action is often distinctive: discussing the hippocampus is naturally tied to the lecture theatre, whereas refilling a water bottle is tied to the kitchenette. These events are meaningful, overlap little, and we do not usually bounce back and forth between them. Wen and Egner conjectured that, outside the laboratory, an item's source, defined as the event in which it was encoded, may be readily available when the item is encountered again. By contrast, laboratory paradigms typically operationalise event boundaries by repeatedly shifting between 'events' that are operationalized as task demands or perceptual features across trials, such as alternating orienting tasks, stimulus category, or stimulus features (DuBrow & Davachi, 2014; Heusser et al., 2018; Sols et al., 2017), so that it is harder to retrieve the source of test pairs. In their first and second experiments, Wen and Egner (2022) aimed to capture the essence of everyday experience by making the encoding context more unique and tightly bound to the object, so that the stimulus itself provided information about its source at retrieval. This is analogous to how the topic "hippocampus" may cue the original lecture when returning to the same lecture theatre. In their first experiment, participants encoded stimuli that were naturally tied to non-repeating orienting tasks (e.g. classifying pictures or solving maths problems), so that each event was defined through the unique combination of the stimulus and orienting task.

Temporal order memory of tested items was more accurate for cross-boundary than within-event pairs (88% vs. 71%), a "flipped" effect. In Experiment 2, they observed the flipped effect across higher-order boundaries involving changes in both stimulus category and task, but the classic within-event advantage across lower-order boundaries involving task changes alone. Their interpretation was that the effect of event boundaries on temporal order memory is not solely due to the perception of event boundaries at encoding, but also to retrieval processes. In their Experiments 3-4, they used a paradigm from Heusser et al. (2018), where participants encoded objects presented within coloured frames and were asked to imagine the object in its respective frame colour and decide whether the object-colour pair was aesthetically pleasing. Events corresponded to short sub-sequences of objects surrounded by a frame of the same colour, which never repeated within the sequence. At test, objects were presented either with or without their original frames. With frames present, they observed the same flipped effect, but its magnitude was more modest, with the difference between cross-and within-boundary items only significant in experiment 3 (70% vs. 67%). The interaction between frame presence and boundary condition was also significant in Experiment 4, due to the presence of the classic effect only in the contextabsent condition.

As mentioned in the introduction, in a critical test of their hypothesis (Experiment 4), remembering the frame colour associated with the test pairs in the source-absent condition did not improve temporal memory, suggesting that access to source identity may not be sufficient on its own to explain the flipped effect. It is possible that Wen and Egner did not observe significant effects of source memory on temporal memory because coloured frames were not sufficiently distinctive, not strongly bound to each object, or both. We hypothesised that in more ecologically-valid paradigm, we would obtain the classic effects in the "source absent" condition, while in the "source present" condition, retrieval processes -specifically, source memory and event-order memory -may outweigh the effects of event boundaries on encoding processes, resulting in a flipped effect on temporal order memory accuracy.

To test this hypothesis, in Experiment 1 (pre-registered on (OSF) 10.17605/OSF.IO/MZ5W6) we conceptually replicate Wen and Egner's (2022) study using more distinct events and attempted to strengthen item-to-context binding by requiring participants to respond to event-specific encoding questions. Our paradigm was designed to capture the more ecologically valid task they employed in their first two experiments, where the magnitude of the effect was larger, but corresponded in other procedural details to their Experiment 4, including the manipulation of source presence and the inclusion of a source memory test. Wen and Egner (2022) suggested that using distinct, non-recurring event reminders, i.e. coloured frames, and reinstating them at retrieval would produce a "flipped" effect, i.e. better temporal order memory across than within events, and maintain a "classic" effect of event boundaries on temporal distance ratings in both source-present and source-absent conditions. We hypothesised that we will replicate these results and extend them, showing that when event reminders are not presented at test, accurate source memory will result in better temporal order memory.

Method

Participants

Sixty-two healthy young adults (28 females, 34 males, age range 18-44 years, M = 27.10, SD = 6.92), were recruited from the University of Cambridge's online participant pool, SONA (https://cam.sona-systems.com). Participants were compensated £10 per hour for their time.

Individuals with a history of mental health or neurological disorders, or those taking medications known to affect brain function, were excluded from participation.

Participants were randomly assigned to the source-present and source-absent groups. Due to participant dropout during recruitment, the final group sizes were uneven, resulting in 33 participants in the source-absent group and 29 in the source-present group.

Participant exclusion criteria included both preregistered and additional data quality checks. The preregistered criteria specified the exclusion of participants whose temporal order memory accuracy was at or below chance level (≤ 50%) or who failed embedded attention checks. To further ensure data quality, we additionally excluded participants whose temporal order accuracy rates or temporal distance judgments fell more than 1.5 interquartile ranges below the first quartile or above the third quartile. Participants with a mean distance rating of zero were also removed, as this indicated non-engagement with the task. These exclusion criteria were the same across the four experiments. A total of 15 participants were excluded: eight for performing at or below chance level on the temporal order memory task, five whose mean distance rating was 0, and one whose distance ratings fell more than 1.5 interquartile ranges below the first quartile or above the third quartile. All procedures were approved by the University of Cambridge Psychology Research Ethics Committee.

Materials

A total of 252 neutral-coloured object images were selected from the O-Minds database (https://github.com/DuncanLab/OMINDS). All images were pre-processed to appear as squares with a resolution of 500 × 500 pixels. Additionally, 42 location images were generated using ChatGPT at a resolution of 525 × 407 pixels. These images represented six locations in seven places: a museum, a park, a house, a university campus, a shopping mall, a gym, and a hotel. For example, the museum locations comprised a café, art gallery, fossil room, astronomy exhibition room, gift shop, and sculpture room (Figure 1A).

Each of the 42 location images was paired with a location-specific encoding question.

Event boundaries were created by changing the location image and its associated encoding question. Questions targeted either the physical characteristics of objects (e.g., size, weight, or material) or their probabilistic or functional use (e.g., the likelihood of using the object in a particular location or in a specific way). For each space, three questions were written for probabilistic use and three for physical characteristics.

Within each space, questions were written to avoid repetition in linguistic structure (e.g., no two questions used the same verb). All questions were designed to produce a reasonable mix of "yes" and "no" responses, with at least 10% of each expected across participants. Questions that appeared bizarre or emotionally evocative were excluded. For example, for the museum café location, the encoding question was: "Can this be stored inside a fridge display in a museum café?"

Procedure

The experiment included seven rounds. In each round participants took part in an encoding task, a distractor task, and two temporal memory tests. The first round was considered practice and was not analysed. In the final experimental round, the source-absent group completed a source memory test, and all participants then completed a event-order test.

Specifically, repeated source and event-order memory tests could encourage participants, particularly in the source-absent group, to adopt strategies that emphasized encoding and retrieving source information, thereby reducing the impact of the source manipulation. To minimize strategy changes across rounds, we restricted these tests to the final round.

Encoding task

In each round, participants encoded one sequence of objects. Each sequence mimicked a visit to six locations in one of the place, for example, a museum. In each of these locations, participants encoded six objects by answering the encoding question associated with that location. Thus, each sequence consisted of 36 trials, in which participants encoded a combination of one location image, one object image, and its associated encoding question, displayed for 6 seconds. The location image was presented centrally on the screen, with the object displayed below it, and the encoding question shown above (Figure 1C). Participants were asked to respond "yes" or "no" to each question related to the object-location pairing by pressing J for "Yes" or K for "No"). An event was defined as a sequence of consecutive images that shared the same location image and encoding question. Since each encoding sequence contained six different location images and corresponding encoding questions, each sequence was divided into six events.

The order of the seven places was randomized across participants. Within each sequence the order of locations and the objects allocated to each location was also randomized across participants.

Distractor Task

Following the encoding task, participants completed a 30-second distractor task designed to prevent rehearsal and eliminate potential working memory effects. During this task, two ninecharacter alphanumeric strings (e.g., m5y8p2q1b) were presented sequentially for 15 seconds each, and participants were required to select the option displaying each string in reverse order.

After completing the distractor tasks, participants proceeded to the memory tests.

Memory tests

The first test was a temporal order memory test, in which participants were shown two images and asked to select the one that appeared earlier (Figure 1D). Next, they completed a temporal distance judgment test, where they estimated how many images had appeared between the images in each pair (Figure 1E). During both temporal memory tests, participants in the source-present group were shown the objects with their associated location images and encoding question. In contrast, participants in the source-absent group were shown only the object itself.

22 of the 36 objects participants encoded during the study phase were selected to form 11 object pairs for the test phase. The object pairs fell into four conditions: (1) within-event, distance of 2; (2) within-event, distance of 3; (3) cross-boundary, distance of 2; and (4) cross-boundary, distance of 3.

In the within-event conditions, both items in a pair were encoded with the same question and location image. In the cross-boundary conditions, the items were associated with different encoding questions and location images. The distance refers to the number of objects that appeared between the two objects in each pair during encoding.

To avoid potential biases, boundary location images, the first images of each event, which typically require longer encoding times and are better remembered, were excluded from pair selection. The remaining images were randomly selected to form item pairs for each condition (Figure 1B).

In the final experimental round, after the temporal order and distance tasks, participants completed one or two additional memory tests depending on their group assignment (Figure 1F).

Those in the source-absent group completed a source memory test to assess their memory for the event associated with each object. In each source memory trial, participants were shown an object along with the six location images and corresponding encoding questions from the final round. The encoding question appeared above its respective location image. Participants were required to identify which location image had been associated with the object. The six locationquestion pairs were presented in random order.

After completing the previous tasks, both groups completed a event-order test. In this task, the six location-encoding question pairs from the final round were presented in random order, and participants were asked to reconstruct the order in which they originally appeared during encoding (Figure 1F). Following this, participants were asked to report the percentage of time they relied on event-order memory to make their temporal judgments. All memory tasks were self-paced, allowing participants to carefully assess their memory.

We pre-registered mixed-effects models to examine how source availability and boundary conditions influence temporal order accuracy and temporal distance ratings. The models included source availability (source-absent vs. source-present), boundary condition (within-event vs. cross-boundary), and their interaction as fixed effects, with participant entered as a random intercept.

We additionally pre-registered exploratory analyses involving source memory, which was assessed only in the source-absent group. To examine the effects of source memory and boundary on accuracy and distance ratings, a mixed-effects model was fitted. Source memory was categorized based on whether participants remembered neither, one, or both locationquestion pairs associated with the two displayed objects. In this model, source memory (neither vs. one. vs. both) and boundary were entered as fixed effects, with participant as a random intercept.

In addition to these pre-registered analyses, we conducted a non-preregistered analysis examining whether objective distance influenced temporal distance ratings. Objective distance was defined as the number of intervening items between the two tested objects ((2 vs. 3). In this model, boundary, source availability, objective distance, and their interactions were entered as fixed effects, with participant included as a random intercept.

The Supplementary Information reports additional analyses of encoding reaction times across serial positions within an event and their relationship with temporal distance judgments (Supplementary Figure 1), together with descriptive data on participants' self-reported reliance on event-order memory during temporal judgments (Supplementary Table 1).

All data analyses were conducted using R (version 4.3.1) within RStudio, with mixed models implemented in the lme4 package. For all models, an ANOVA was performed to evaluate the significance of the fixed effects and their interactions. For all experiments, data, and analysis code will be available on OSF at https://osf.io/4dfzj/.

Results

Temporal order memory

Boundary and source availability. Temporal order memory accuracy is shown in Figure 2A. Accuracy was higher for within-event than cross-boundary trials in both the source-absent and source-present conditions, although this difference appeared larger in the source-absent condition. The analysis revealed a significant main effect of boundary, F(1, 46) = 37.00, p < .001, ηₚ² =.45. There was also a significant main effect of source availability, F(1, 46) = 9.30, p = .003, ηₚ² =.18. In addition, a significant boundary x source availability interaction was observed, F(1, 46) = 9.09, p = .005, ηₚ² =.16. Post hoc Tukey-adjusted comparisons revealed that in the source-absent condition, accuracy was significantly higher for within-event trials than crossboundary trials, t(46) = 6.16, p < .001, d = 1.86. In the source-present condition, the boundary effect was smaller but remained significant, with higher accuracy for within-event than crossboundary trials, t(46) = 2.29, p = .027, d = 0.63.

Source memory and boundary in the source-absent condition.

There was a significant main effect of source memory, F(2, 80) = 9.66, p < .001, ηₚ² = .19. Accuracy increased with the number of sources correctly remembered for the tested pairs. The main effect of boundary was not significant, F(1, 80) = 1.27, p = .264, ηₚ² =.02, nor was the boundary x source memory interaction, F(2, 80) = 0.02, p = .985, ηₚ² < .01 (Figure 2C).

Temporal distance judgements

Boundary and source availability. Temporal distance ratings are shown in Figure 2B.

Cross-boundary pairs were rated as farther apart than within-event pairs in both the source-absent and source-present conditions. Ratings were generally lower in the source-present condition than in the source-absent condition. The analysis revealed a significant main effect of boundary, F(1, 46) = 145.27, p < .001, ηₚ² = .76. There was also a significant main effect of source availability, F(1, 46) = 6.93, p = .012, ηₚ² =.13. The boundary x source availability interaction was not significant, F(1, 46) = 1.17, p = .285, ηₚ² = .02.

Source memory and boundary in the source-absent condition.

The analysis revealed a significant main effect of boundary, F(1, 61.50) = 7.91, p = .007, ηₚ² = .11, replicating the effect reported above. The main effect of source memory did not reach significance, F(2, 64.96) = 2.66, p = .078, ηₚ² = .08. The boundary x source memory interaction was also not significant, F(2, 61.41) = 2.94, p = .060, ηₚ² = .09. To further examine the boundary effect when source memory was accurate, we restricted the analysis to trials where participants correctly identified the sources of both items. This revealed a significant main effect of boundary, F(1, 20.35) = 36.92, p < .001, ηₚ² = .68 (Figure 2D).

Objective distance.

Consistent with our other analyses, the model revealed a significant main effect of boundary, F(1, 138) = 284.93, p < .001, ηₚ² = .67, a significant main effect of source availability, F(1, 46) = 6.99, p = .011, ηₚ² = .13. The boundary by source availability interaction was not significant, F(1, 138) = 2.30, p = .132, ηₚ² = .02. There was no main effect of objective distance, F(1, 138) = 0.40, p = .526, ηₚ² < .01. Objective distance also did not interact significantly with boundary, F(1, 138) = 0.49, p = .825, ηₚ² < .01, or source availability, F(1, 138) = 0.96, p = .328, ηₚ² < .01. The three-way interaction among boundary, source availability, and objective distance was also not significant, F(1, 138) = 0.00, p = .962, ηₚ² < .01.

Discussion

This experiment conceptually replicated Wen and Egner (2022) but did not find the "flipped effect", namely, better temporal order memory across event boundaries than withinevents when event reminders are presented at test. Like Wen and Egner, we used non-recurring events and presented event reminders at retrieval. If anything, our events were more distinctive and item-event associations were encoded more deeply than in the paradigm they employed in their first two experiments, and certainly more than those employed in their last two experiments. Nevertheless, we observed the classic within-event advantage in both source-present and sourceabsent conditions, both in temporal order memory and in temporal distance ratings, challenging the claim that distinct event reminders at retrieval can flip the classic effect of event segmentation on temporal order memory. The distance dilation in both source conditions matched our preregistered prediction, although we did not reproduce Wen and Egner's (2022) finding that source presence increased the magnitude of this effect.

Notably, our results support the hypothesis that source memory influences temporal order memory. First, replicating Wen and Egner's findings in their Experiments 3 and 4, when sources were present during retrieval, the boundary effect was reduced, since cross-boundary item-order accuracy improved in the source-present condition. Crucially, extending their work, our results supported the critical hypothesis in their fourth experiment, which their original results failed to support: here, temporal order memory also improved when participants in the source-absent condition correctly remembered the sources associated with more items in the pair, suggesting that our methodological changes may have helped participants remember event order. Experiment 2 examines this possibility in greater depth.

For temporal distance ratings in our source-absent condition, neither the main effect of source memory nor the Source Memory x Boundary interaction reached significance, whereas Wen and Egner's (2022) Experiment 4 reported both effects in an analysis combining sourcepresent and source-absent conditions. Although we did not register a hypothesis about objective distance between tested pairs, we had assumed that lag will influence temporal distance ratings.

The absence of this effect was surprising, given that boundary crossing increased perceived distance by roughly four items. Within retrieved-context models, this is difficult to explain as a purely encoding-driven increase in context drift, because it would require context drift at a boundary to be much larger than the drift produced by encoding a number of additional items.

Together, these results motivate a post-encoding account in which not only order memory but also distance judgments are biased by retrieved item-event associations. Experiment 2 tested this conjecture more directly.

Experiment 2

In Experiment 1 we limited ourselves to testing source memory only at the very end of the session to minimise strategy shifts in temporal inference across earlier rounds. This design choice only allowed us to collect data on source memory for items encoded in the final round.

However, to further examine how retrieval processes shape temporal memory it is useful to have more robust data on source memory -both associative memory for the source in which test objects were encoded (as in Experiment 1) as well as on memory for event order. This information can only be obtained when the source is not presented at test. Therefore, Experiment 2 (OSF 10.17605/OSF.IO/SYHTA) focused on the source-absent condition of Experiment 1, employing the typical event-segmentation memory-test set-up, without event reminders at test. Each encoding round was followed by a test of source and event-order memory. Following Experiment 1, we hypothesized that, for cross-boundary pairs, the relationship between source memory and temporal order memory would depend on event-order memory.

Because temporal distance ratings in Experiment 1 depended on source information at retrieval (higher when the source was absent) but not on objective distance at encoding (2 vs. 3 intervening items), we speculated that they, too, may depend on source retrieval. We

Method

Participants

Forty healthy adults (21 female, 19 male), aged 20-39 years (M = 25.93, SD = 4.70), were recruited through the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf participant database.

Participant exclusion followed preregistered criteria documented on the OSF (10.17605/OSF.IO/SYHTA).

Materials

In Study 2, the materials were the same as in Study 1, with two exceptions: the encoding questions were translated into German, and the location images were selected from Google Images. The image set depicted the same six locations within each place as in Study 1. All location images were pre-processed to a resolution of 1356 × 1089 pixels.

Procedure

Experiment 2 was conducted as an fMRI study; however, the present paper focuses only on the behavioural results. Analyses of the neural data will be reported separately. The overall procedure was the same as the source-absent condition in Experiment 1, but the timing and display format of both the encoding and temporal memory tasks were modified to accommodate fMRI data acquisition. In addition, source memory and event order memory tasks were added at the end of each round, following the temporal memory tasks.

Encoding task

During encoding, the object and location image were presented together for 4s, with a fixation cross displayed at the centre of the object. The encoding question was displayed below the images only on the first encoding trial of each event; for the remaining five trials within that event, the question was not shown during the 4s object-location display. Participants were instructed to maintain fixation on the central cross and view the images without moving their eyes, to minimise gaze-related noise for the intended multivariate pattern analyses of the fMRI data. This fixation requirement was waived on the first trial of each event, when a new event was introduced, so that participants could look at the location image and read the associated encoding question. Each encoding trial then included a 2s fixation cross, a 1.5s presentation of the question alone, a 1s blank screen, and a final 0.5s fixation cross.

Memory tests

For the temporal memory tests, each trial began with a 2s blank screen and a 1s fixation cross, followed by a 4s presentation of the image pair with a fixation cross between the two images. After this initial viewing period, the same image pair remained on the screen, without the fixation cross, while participants first made a self-paced temporal order judgment, followed by a self-paced temporal distance judgment.

Finally, after completing the temporal memory tests in each round, participants completed a self-paced source memory task and a event-order memory task.

Data analysis

To test our preregistered hypothesis that source memory and event-memory jointly influence temporal order accuracy on cross-boundary trials, we fit a mixed-effects model with event-order memory accuracy (accurate vs. inaccurate), source memory accuracy (neither vs. one vs. both), and their interaction as fixed effects, with participant included as a random intercept. This analysis was restricted to cross-boundary trials because remembering the order of events is only informative when the two items come from different sources; for within-event trials, both items share the same source, so event-order memory is not defined and cannot contribute to the judgment. Event-order memory accuracy was defined as whether participants correctly remembered which of the two sources associated with the tested items had occurred first, based on their reconstruction of full event sequence in the event-order memory task.

We also preregistered an analysis examining whether encoded-retrieved boundary consistency, defined as the match between the encoded boundary condition (within vs. cross) and the retrieved boundary condition (within vs. cross), together with objective distance (2 vs. 3), predicts temporal distance judgments. Retrieved boundary was classified from the source reports collected after the temporal judgments: pairs assigned to the same source were classified as within-event, and pairs assigned to different sources as cross-boundary. Finally, for completion, we repeated this analysis using temporal order memory, which was not registered.

Results

Temporal order memory

Encoded-retrieved boundary consistency. Figure 3A shows temporal order memory accuracy as a function of encoded and retrieved boundary. Accuracy was higher when the retrieved boundary matched the encoded boundary: encoded within-event pairs were remembered more accurately when retrieved as within-event than as cross-boundary, whereas encoded cross-boundary pairs were remembered more accurately when retrieved as crossboundary than as within-event. The analysis showed significant main effects for both retrieved boundary, χ²(1) = 10.24, p = .001, and encoded boundary, χ²(1) = 10.77, p = .001, as well as a significant interaction between retrieved boundary and encoded boundary, χ²(1) = 9.24, p = .002.

No other main effects or interactions, including those involving objective distance, reached statistical significance (all ps > .60). Post hoc pairwise comparisons (Tukey-adjusted) showed that temporal order memory was higher when participants retrieved-boundary condition matched the encoded-boundary condition. Specifically, for item pairs encoded within an event, accuracy was higher when participants retrieved the pair as within-event rather than cross-boundary (OR = 3.21, SE = 0.34, z = 10.89, p < .001). Conversely, for item pairs encoded across a boundary, accuracy was higher when participants retrieved the pair as cross-boundary rather than withinevent (OR = 0.38, SE = 0.05, z = -8.07, p < .001).

Source memory and event-order memory.

Figure 3C demonstrates the effect of source memory and event-order memory on temporal order memory for cross-boundary pairs. The analysis revealed that neither the main effect of source memory, χ²(2) = 0.18, p = .915, nor the main effect of event-order memory, χ²(1) = 0.60, p = .440, was statistically significant. However, the interaction between source memory and event-order memory was significant, χ²(2) = 36.74, p < .001. Tukey-adjusted post hoc comparisons showed that, when participants incorrectly remembered the event order, temporal order memory accuracy did not differ across source memory levels (all ps ≥ .911). When event-order memory was correct, accuracy did not differ between trials in which participants remembered neither source and trials in which they correctly remembered one source (OR = 0.93, SE = 0.14, z = -0.49, p = .875). In contrast, trials in which participants correctly remembered both sources differed from trials in which they correctly remembered neither source (OR = 0.25, SE = 0.04, z = -8.80, p < .001) and one source (OR = 0.27, SE = 0.03, z = -11.83, p < .001; Figure 3C).

Temporal distance judgment

Effect of retrieved boundary. Figure 3B shows temporal distance ratings as a function of encoded and retrieved boundary. Participants rated pairs as farther apart when they retrieved them as cross-boundary than when they retrieved them as within-event. This pattern was observed for both encoded within-event and encoded cross-boundary pairs. We found a significant main effect of retrieved boundary on temporal distance judgments, F(1, 5217.40) = 9.95, p = .002, ηₚ² < .01. When participants retrieved pairs as within-event, temporal distance ratings were lower than when they retrieved pairs as cross-boundary. The main effects of encoded boundary, F(1, 5213.50) = 1.44, p = .230, ηₚ² < .01, and objective distance, F(1, 5212.70) = 0.00, p = .964, ηₚ² < .01, were not significant. The interaction between retrieved boundary and encoded boundary was also not significant, F(1, 5217.20) = 3.28, p = .070 ηₚ² < .01, nor were any of the other interactions (all ps ≥ .311; partial η²s < .01).

Discussion

Consistent with our hypothesis and extending conclusions from Experiment 1, source memory supported temporal order judgments for cross-boundary pairs only when participants also remembered event order. When event order was incorrect, temporal order accuracy did not vary with the number of sources remembered correctly. When event order was correct, accuracy was higher when participants remembered both item sources than when they remembered only one or neither. This pattern suggests that cross-boundary temporal order judgments benefit most when participants can identify both sources and remember their order. Strikingly, retrieved boundary, but not encoded boundary, was associated with temporal distance judgments. Pairs reported as belonging to different events were rated as farther apart than pairs judged as belonging to the same event, whereas effects of encoded boundary and objective distance were not significant. This pattern is consistent with the hypothesis that temporal distance judgments draw on reconstructed event structure, with items assigned to different events judged farther apart in time.

Together, these results suggest that temporal memory is not a direct read-out of event segmentation during encoding, but depends critically on associative retrieval, with different dependencies for within-and cross-boundary pairs for temporal order memory.

Experiment 3

Experiment 2 demonstrated that accurate temporal order memory depends jointly on item-event associations and memory for the order of the relevant sources. However, because event-order memory was not experimentally controlled in Experiment 2, these results could be due to pre-experimental individual differences. Additionally, differing from the typical event segmentation paradigms, in Experiment 2 we administered the source and event-order memory tasks after each round, a decision which may have induced strategy shifts across rounds, specifically increased reliance on source information when making temporal judgments.

To address these limitations, Experiment 3 (pre-registered on OSF 10.17605/OSF.IO/6XVBF) manipulated the number of events within each encoding sequence (three, as in Wen and Egner's experiment 1, vs. six, as in their experiments 3-4). We assumed that having only three, rather than six, events within each sequence would render event-order easier to remember. This time, we employed the source-present condition of Experiment 1 to better control item-event associations at retrieval and more directly test the contribution of eventorder memory to temporal memory. We hypothesized that the effect of boundary on temporal order memory would differ by sequence structure. Compared to within-boundary pairs, we hypothesised that accuracy would be poorer the 6-event condition, reflecting a classic effect and replicating previous results, but better in the 3-event condition, reflecting a flipped effect. For temporal distance memory, we again predicted a classic effect.

Method

Participants

Fifty-five healthy adults (25 female, 30 male), aged 20 to 45 years (M = 31.95, SD = 6.84), were recruited via Prolific and received £10 per hour for their participation. Four participants were excluded from data analysis: three due to chance-level performance on the temporal order memory task, and one whose temporal distance ratings were more than 1.5 interquartile ranges beyond the first or third quartile. All exclusion criteria followed preregistered guidelines documented on the OSF.

Materials

We used the same object images, location images, and randomisation rules as in Experiment 1 to construct the encoding sequences but manipulated sequence structure by varying the number of events per sequence. Two sequence types were created: six-event sequences and three-event sequences. In both sequence types, each sequence was drawn from a single place category (museum, park, house, university campus, shopping mall, gym, or hotel), and the order of events within each sequence, as well as the order of sequences, was fully randomized.

Six-event sequences contained six events, each paired with six object images, as in Experiment 1. Three-event sequences contained three events randomly selected from the six possible events within the same place category, each paired with 12 object images. For six-event sequences, tested pairs were selected as in Experiment 1, whereas each three-event sequence included eight tested pairs: two within-event and two cross-boundary pairs separated by two intervening items, and two within-event and two cross-boundary pairs separated by three intervening items.

Procedure

Experiment 3 included only the source-present condition, in which participants saw each object together with its associated location image and encoding question during the temporal memory tasks. Participants were randomly assigned to either the three-event or six-event group.

In the three-event group, each encoding sequence comprised three events, whereas in the six-event group each sequence comprised six events. All other procedures were identical to Experiment 1.

Data analysis

We pre-registered analyses testing whether temporal order accuracy and temporal distance ratings vary as a function of sequence structure and boundary type, using mixed-effects models. Each model included sequence structure (three-event vs. six-event ), boundary (withinevent vs. cross-boundary), and their interaction as fixed effects, with participant included as a random intercept. For these preregistered models, we used ANOVA to test the significance of fixed effects and their interactions.

In a non-registered analysis motivated by Pu et al. (2022),we examined within-event and cross-boundary pairs sharing local positions. First, in the six-event condition we compared pairs where one item was in local position 2 and the other from local position 5, comparing withinboundary pairs (the earlier probe in position 2 and the later probe in position 5) to acrossboundary pairs (the early probe in position 5 and the late probe in position 2 of the next event).

Second, in the 3-event condition we compared pairs where one probe was in local position 4. Here, we compared cross-boundary pairs where the other probe was in local position 12 of the previous event to within-boundary pairs where the other probe was in local position 8 in the same event. While the number of intervening items was held constant in this comparison, the pairs had two intervening items in the six-event comparison and three in the three-event comparison, and therefore the two conditions could not be compared directly.

For these two boundary comparisons, we fitted separate binomial mixed-effects models with a logit link, boundary as a fixed effect, and a participant random intercept. We used twosided Wald tests, with Holm correction across the two comparisons, and report odds ratios with 95% Wald confidence intervals. Descriptive accuracies were averaged first within participants and then across participants contributing to each condition. As a sensitivity analysis, we calculated percentile 95% confidence intervals for the accuracy differences from 20,000 bootstrap samples, resampling participants together with all their responses.

Results

Temporal order memory

Boundary and sequence structure. Figure 4A shows temporal order memory accuracy as a function of sequence structure and boundary. Accuracy was higher for cross-boundary than within-event pairs in the three-event condition, but higher for within-event than cross-boundary pairs in the six-event condition. We found a significant boundary x sequence structure interaction, F(1, 49) = 50.70, p < .001, ηₚ² = .51. The main effect of boundary was marginal, F(1, 49) = 4.02, p = .050, ηₚ² = .08, and the main effect of sequence structure was not significant, F(1, 49) = 3.35, p = .073, ηₚ² = .06. Post hoc Tukey-adjusted comparisons indicated that the boundary effect differed across sequence structures. In the three-event group, accuracy was significantly higher for cross-boundary trials than within-event trials, t(49) = -6.80, p < .001, d = 1.82. In contrast, in the six-event group, accuracy was significantly higher for within-event trials than cross-boundary trials, t(49) = 3.45, p = .001, d = 1.02.

Event order memory.

We pre-registered a prediction that reducing the number of events would make event order easier to remember. Given this directional prediction, we compared relative event-order performance between the three-and six-event groups using a one-tailed Welch's t test. Performance was significantly higher in the three-event than in the six-event group, t(47.17) = 1.76, p = .042, Cohen's d = 0.48. However, event order memory was overall poor, and was not significantly better than chance in any of the groups (see Supplementary information).

Exploratory analysis.

To examine whether the flipped boundary effect in the three-event condition could be explained by differences in local position, we compared cross-boundary pairs from position 12 and position 4 of the next event with within-event pairs from positions 4 and 8. Both pair types included an item from local position 4 and had the same temporal lag, while the unmatched item occupied a later local position in the cross-boundary pair (position 12) than in the within-event pair (position 8). Nevertheless, temporal order memory was more accurate for cross-boundary than within-event pairs, χ²(1) = 6.51, OR = 3.13, 95% CI [1.30, 7.54], Holm-adjusted p = .021.

The participant-bootstrap analysis showed a mean accuracy difference of .12, 95% CI [-.02, .29].

For the six-event condition, we compared within-event pairs from positions 2 and 5 with cross-boundary pairs from position 5 and position 2 of the next event. This comparison matched local positions between the within-event and cross-boundary pairs while reversing their chronological roles. Temporal order memory was more accurate for within-event than crossboundary pairs, χ²(1) = 5.79, OR = 1.97, 95% CI [1.13, 3.42], Holm-adjusted p = .021. The participant-bootstrap analysis showed a mean accuracy difference of .11, 95% CI [.02, .20].

Temporal distance judgment

Boundary and sequence structure. Figure 4B shows temporal distance ratings as a function of sequence structure and boundary. Cross-boundary pairs were rated as farther apart than within-event pairs in both the three-event and six-event conditions, although ratings were higher overall in the three-event condition than in the six-event condition. The analysis showed a significant main effect of boundary on distance ratings, F(1, 49) = 118.60, p < .001, ηₚ² = .71, replicated the finding from experiment 1. There was also a significant main effect of sequence structure, F(1, 49) = 4.80, p = .033, ηₚ² = .09. The boundary x sequence structure interaction was not significant, F(1, 49) = 2.76, p = .103, ηₚ² = .05.

Discussion

Experiment 3 showed more accurate temporal order memory for cross-boundary than within-event pairs in the three-event condition. We observed the classic pattern in the six-event group, with better temporal order memory for within-event than for cross-boundary pairs, but a "flipped" pattern in the three-event group. Fewer, longer events can make event positions easier to distinguish while making positions within events harder to distinguish. This shift can favour cross-boundary over within-event judgments even when the precision of the retrieval process remains unchanged. Because source information was available at retrieval in both conditions, the six-event result also challenges the claim that source information at retrieval necessarily flips the effect of event segmentation on temporal order memory (Wen & Egner, 2022). The results in the six-event condition replicate Experiment 1. Both experiments used distinctive events but did not produce the flipped effect, suggesting that event distinctiveness alone is also insufficient.

Together with Experiment 2, these findings support a retrieval account in which sequence structure shapes how event and item information contribute to temporal judgments.

In this experiment, we expected and found that event order memory would be better in the three-versus the six-event condition, but performance was overall poor. Like Experiment 1, but unlike Experiment 2, the test of event order memory was incidental and was administered only for events from the last round. Relative event-order accuracy did not differ significantly from chance in the three-event group and was significantly below chance in the six-event group. Therefore, while sequence structure changed the boundary effect, this experiment provided only limited evidence that better retrieval of event order explained the reversal of the within-event advantage.

To keep the duration and effort of encoding the same, the manipulation of the number of events in this experiment was necessarily confounded with the length of events. Because Pu et al. (2022) showed that temporal order memory is more accurate for items encoded earlier within an event, it is reasonable to consider whether present results are due a local position confound.

While the sequences were not designed to test this question, we could compare, for the six-event condition, test pairs where the early probe was in position 2 and the late in position 5 of the same event (denoted "2-5"), to pairs where the early probe was in position 5 and the late probe in position 2 of the next event (denoted "5-2"). This comparison, which eliminates potential confounding effects of local position, showed higher accuracy for within-event pairs, suggesting that the classic effect observed in this condition was not confounded. In the three-event condition a perfect comparison was not possible, but a reasonably close match was a comparison between the cross-boundary pairs "12-4" versus the within-boundary pair "4-8" (both with a lag of 3).

Cross-boundary pairs were ordered more accurately despite having a second item in the pair occupying a later local position. A simple early-position advantage for that item would predict the opposite pattern. Future work could replicate the reversed effect of event segmentation on temporal-order judgement in sequences designed to control local positions.

For temporal distance judgments, we replicated the classic effect. Additionally, participants in the three-event group gave larger temporal distance ratings than those in the sixevent group, an effect that is difficult to attribute to encoding processes alone. Again, this effect aligns with a heuristic that items encoded within longer events (12 vs. 6 items in the 3-event vs. the 6-event group) are likely to be farther apart. Experiment 4 was conducted to examine this possibility.

Experiment 4

Experiment 4 (pre-registered on OSF (10.17605/OSF.IO/E7GPJ) was designed to focus on the role of retrieval processes in temporal distance judgements. In Experiment 2 temporal distance judgments were driven primarily by retrieved boundary structure than by the objective boundary condition at encoding. However, because we did not control the information participants had at retrieval, it remained unclear whether reconstructed source information caused the observed effects. Experiment 4 therefore experimentally manipulated source information at retrieval. To do so, we provided correct or incorrect cues about the encoding source of a small number of test pairs. While the majority of event reminders were correct, some test pairs that were encoded within events were cued by different events, while some test pairs that were encoded across events were cued by the same event. This design allowed us to directly test how what participants believe at retrieval influences temporal distance judgments.

We hypothesized that the effect of the objective boundary condition at encoding on temporal distance ratings would depend on retrieval boundary information: objectively crossboundary pairs would be judged as less distant when the cues suggest they were encoded within the same event, whereas objectively within-boundary pairs would be judged as more distant when the cues suggest they were encoded in two different events. We further hypothesized that, as in Experiment 2, temporal order memory would be higher when retrieval boundary information was correct than when it was incorrect.

Method

Participants

Forty-eight healthy adults were recruited via Prolific and were paid £10 per hour for their participation. Ten participants who reported noticing mismatches between items and their associated encoding-event reminders were excluded, leaving a final sample of 38 healthy adults aged 21 to 44 years (M = 30.66, SD = 6.16), including 21 females and 17 males. Because the study tested how the accuracy of retrieved source information influences temporal memory, awareness of these mismatches could have undermined the intended manipulation of retrieval boundary information (correct vs. incorrect). In addition, two participants were excluded from the temporal order memory analysis because their performance was at chance level. These exclusion criteria were specified in the OSF preregistration.

Materials

We used the same object images, location images, and sequence-construction rules as in Experiment 1, except that, in the experimental rounds, some tested pairs were presented with incorrect source information at retrieval.

In the temporal memory tasks, two trials per round were selected to contain incorrect source information: one from a within-boundary pair and one from a cross-boundary pair.

Within-boundary pairs consisted of two items encoded within the same event and separated by either a distance of 2 (W2) or 3 (W3), whereas cross-boundary pairs consisted of two items encoded across different events and separated by either a distance of 2 (C2) or 3 (C3). Across the six experimental rounds, selection was balanced such that W2 and W3 trials were each selected three times, and C2 and C3 trials were each selected three times.

The source-swap rule depended on pair type. For W2 and W3 trials, which were originally within-boundary, the source information for one item in the pair was replaced with that of an adjacent event in the presentation sequence, either the preceding or following event, so that the pair appeared cross-boundary at retrieval. If the swapped object originally belonged to the first event in the sequence, its source was always changed to that of the next event. If the swapped object originally belonged to the last event in the sequence, its source was always changed to that of the previous event.

For C2 and C3 trials, which were originally cross-boundary, the source information for one item was replaced with the other item's encoding source, so that the pair appeared withinboundary at retrieval. Across rounds, swaps were balanced such that, in each round, one incorrect-source trial involved changing the source information of the left object and the other involved changing the source information of the right object.

Finally, each round contained six events. To avoid concentrating incorrect-source trials in particular parts of the sequence, the original event position of the swapped object was balanced across the experiment. Across the six experimental rounds, each of the six event positions was selected exactly twice, yielding 12 incorrect-source trials distributed evenly across original event positions.

Procedure

The procedure was identical to that of the source-present condition in Experiment 1, except that, in the temporal memory tasks, selected test trials presented incorrect source information at retrieval. Additionally, at the end of the study, participants were asked to complete the manipulation-check questions: "Did you notice any problems with the questions or images we used in this experiment?" and "Were any of the questions and images mixed up in any way? If yes, please describe the problem in as much detail as possible."

Data analysis

Due to a programming error, 38 of 216 intended within-event manipulation trials did not alter the pair's displayed boundary status. Retrieval boundary information was therefore classified according to the event reminders actually displayed at test. We pre-registered mixedeffects model analyses to examine whether temporal order accuracy and temporal distance ratings differed across the main experimental conditions in the present study. Each model included retrieval boundary information (correct vs. incorrect), objective boundary at encoding (within-event vs. cross-boundary), and their interaction as fixed effects, with participant included as a random intercept. For all models, ANOVA was used to assess the significance of the fixed effects and their interaction.

We also conducted one non-preregistered exploratory analysis. For within-event trials with incorrect retrieval boundary information, we tested whether incorrect temporal order judgments were biased toward the event order shown at test. On these trials, the two objects had originally been encoded within the same event, but one object was presented with a different source at retrieval, making the pair appear cross-boundary. Because the displayed sources had occurred in a particular order during encoding, participants could base their judgment on event order rather than on the objects' true temporal order. For each participant, we calculated the proportion of incorrect responses that were consistent with the displayed event order. This proportion was compared against .50, the level expected if errors were random.

Results

Temporal order memory

Retrieval boundary information and encoded boundary.

Figure 5A shows temporal order memory accuracy across retrieval information and boundary conditions. Accuracy was higher when retrieval information was correct than when it was incorrect. Accuracy was also higher for within-event than cross-boundary pairs, both when retrieval information was correct and when it was incorrect. A mixed-effects model revealed a significant main effect of retrieval boundary information, F(1, 105) = 75.14, p < .001, ηₚ² =.42, indicating that temporal order accuracy differed between trials with correct and incorrect retrieval boundary information. There was also a significant main effect of objective boundary at encoding, F(1,105) = 19.11, p < .001, ηₚ² = .15, such that temporal order accuracy differed between within-event and cross-boundary pairs. The interaction between retrieval boundary information and objective boundary at encoding was not significant, F(1, 105) = 0.33, p = .568, ηₚ² = .03.

Bias toward retrieved event order on within-event trials.

We then tested whether incorrect temporal order judgments on within-event trials with incorrect retrieval boundary information followed the order of the sources shown at test. On these trials, participants made 73 incorrect responses in total, of which 54 were consistent with the event order shown at test and 19 were inconsistent with it. The proportion of errors consistent with the event order shown at test was significantly greater than chance, t(34) = 3.75, p < .001, d = 0.63.

Temporal distance judgment

Retrieval boundary information and encoded boundary. Figure 5B shows temporal distance ratings across retrieval information and boundary conditions. Within-event pairs were rated as closer together than cross-boundary pairs when retrieval information was correct. When retrieval information was incorrect, this pattern reversed: within-event pairs shown as crossboundary were rated as farther apart, whereas cross-boundary pairs shown as within-event were rated as closer together. A mixed-effects model showed a significant interaction between retrieval boundary information and objective boundary at encoding on temporal distance ratings, F(1, 105) = 86.88, p < .001, ηₚ² = .45, indicating that the effect of incorrect retrieval boundary information differed for within-event and cross-boundary pairs. There was also a significant main effect of retrieval boundary information, F(1, 105) = 4.64, p = .034, ηₚ² = .04, whereas the main effect of objective boundary at encoding was not significant, F(1, 105) = 1.63, p = .205, ηₚ² =.02. Follow-up comparisons showed that, for within-event pairs, ratings were significantly lower when retrieval boundary information was correct than when it was incorrect, t(105) = -8.11, p < .001, d = -1.91. In contrast, for cross-boundary pairs, ratings were significantly higher when retrieval boundary information was correct than when it was incorrect, t(105) = 5.07, p < .001, d = 1.19,

Discussion

Experiment 4 directly tested whether retrieval cues, specifically cues that altered participants' beliefs, influenced temporal memory. We found that temporal distance judgments were shaped more by the boundary structure implied at retrieval than by the objective boundary structure at encoding, consistent with our hypothesis. When incorrect event reminders made within-event pairs appear cross-boundary, participants judged them as farther apart. Conversely, when incorrect event reminders made cross-boundary pairs appear within-event, participants judged them as closer together.

Retrieval boundary information did not influence temporal order memory in the same way. Nevertheless, when participants made errors on within-event trials with incorrect retrieval boundary information, they often based their judgments on retrieved event order rather than on the true temporal order of the objects. Together, these findings provide direct evidence that retrieval processes causally influence behavioural markers of event segmentation, particularly temporal distance judgments.

The Hierarchical Context Reconstruction Model

Theories of contextual retrieval allow a cue to identify an episode whose contents are to be recovered. Context supplies a basis for favouring items associated with that episode (Raaijmakers & Shiffrin, 1981). When the appropriate context is no longer active, retrieving the context of a group, list, or event has been proposed as a way to guide search among its contents (Cornell & Zhang, 2025; Farrell, 2012; Jang & Huber, 2008). For example, an instruction identifying a studied list can be represented as a cue that reinstates the list's context before its individual items are recalled (Healey & Wahlheim, 2024). Explaining temporal judgments additionally requires specifying how retrieved information indicates when those contents occurred.

Context-based models have been applied to boundary effects on temporal-order memory (Horner et al., 2016; Peng et al., 2025; Pu et al., 2022) and to the organisation of free recall by events (Lohnas et al., 2023). Neural evidence also connects this retrieval mechanism to event organization: temporal-context patterns reinstated during recall retain differences associated with event boundaries at study (Lohnas et al., 2023). Together with information about the serial position of an item within an event, context-based accounts can explain their influence on temporal order memory accuracy (Peng et al., 2025; Pu et al., 2022). Nevertheless, because these models were designed to simulate classic effects of event segmentation, they cannot explain the flip effects demonstrated in experiments 3 and 4. Accounting for situations in which event reminders are available at retrieval, either endogenously (recalling the lecture theatre influences a judgement of whether the lecturer mentioned the hippocampus or the cortex first) or exogenously (returning to the lecture theatre) thus necessitates a new model.

The Hierarchical Context Reconstruction (HCR) model combines evidence about an object's position within its event with evidence about the event's place in the sequence of events.

An object retrieves information about which event contained it. This information combines with any displayed event reminders to determine which event supplies temporal evidence. When two objects are tested together, the event retrieved for one can also influence the event assigned to the other. Correctly identifying the event can help locate the object in time, whereas misidentifying it can supply evidence about another event. Both order choices and distance ratings depend on the positions reconstructed from this event information and the objects' own temporal evidence.

HCR retains the learned associations between features and context used in Context Maintenance and Retrieval (CMR) models and their applications to memory judgments (Jin et al., 2024; Morton & Polyn, 2016; Polyn et al., 2009). Building on the distinction between temporal context and within-event position in Peng et al. (2025), HCR gives object and event information separate context and memory systems (Figure 6). Global temporal context continues to change across the sequence, while local temporal context restarts at each event boundary.

Objects become associated with their local context and the identity of their event; the recurring event reminders becomes associated with global context throughout the event. These associations allow an object to retrieve evidence about its position within an event and the event to retrieve evidence about its position in the sequence of events. For example, an object studied in the café may be assigned to the café or mistakenly to the gift shop. Several temporal positions can remain possible under either event assignment. HCR weights these possible reconstructions by their probabilities to predict order choices and distance ratings.. HCR uses the probabilities of these alternatives to predict order choices and distance ratings. A displayed event reminder can favour a particular event assignment, changing which event's temporal context is retrieved and the resulting reconstruction of the object's position. Objects Within Events, Events Within a Sequence. Note. (A) Associations supporting temporal reconstruction. An object retrieves local temporal context and evidence about its event's identity, termed source context. Identifying the event provides access to its cue, termed the source feature, which retrieves global temporal context This extension requires both a way to recover an event's context and a rule for interpreting that context as temporal evidence. In HCR, retrieved context supplies temporal evidence through its relationship to position. Positional accounts of serial recall associate items with graded signals relative to a sequence's beginning and end, so the learned associations distinguish where each item belongs in the sequence (Henson, 1998). As context drifts away from its initial state, its overlap with that state can similarly provide a cue to position. Pu et al. (2022) used differences in contextual distance from the beginning of the sequence to judge order and considered extending this principle to distance judgments. Peng et al. (2025) retained the rule for order judgments while separating continuously drifting temporal context from a withinevent position code that restarted at each boundary. HCR builds on these principles to reconstruct positions at both event and object levels.

At each level, HCR compares retrieved support with reference values representing the support expected at each possible position (Figure 7). These values are derived from the study schedule and context trajectories. They decline across positions because later contexts retain less overlap with beginning context. Closer matches between retrieved support and a position's reference value make that position more probable, while allowing several positions to remain plausible. Positions initially selected using these probabilities reinstate context that influences Initial Positional Evidence for Events and Their Contents.
