In B, both objects are assigned to the café, giving greater weight to objects associated with that event. Greater overlap with beginning context generally indicates an earlier position. Coloured lines show retrieved support; grey points and connecting lines show reference values for each possible position. The profiles coincide here because both levels have three candidate positions and the illustrative parameters give the same effective decay between positions. They need not coincide for other settings. Closer matches produce higher initial probabilities for those positions. Model fitting and evaluation

Parameter estimation

We fitted the model jointly to order choices and distance ratings so that both tasks constrain the same account of temporal reconstruction. We used maximum-likelihood estimation, which seeks the parameter values that assign the highest probability to the recorded responses.

This approach follows likelihood-based fitting of retrieved-context models of free recall (Morton & Polyn, 2016). For each experiment, we estimated one set of parameters using all participants' individual responses. Those parameters apply to every condition, including both event schedules in Experiment 3.

For each tested pair, the model assigns probabilities to the participant's order choice and numerical distance rating. In Experiments 1, 3, and 4, the model considers alternative reconstructions of which events contained the items and where they occurred in the sequence.

Each reconstruction contributes according to its probability under the model, supplying the evidence about order and separation used to calculate both response probabilities.. Multiplying these response probabilities across all tested pairs gives the likelihood.. Table 1 reports the fitted log likelihood (LL) and Akaike information criterion (AIC), calculated as twice the number of free parameters minus twice LL.

Experiment 2 also requires the model to generate later source-memory reports, identifying which event contained each object, and event-order reports, giving the remembered order of the events. The model links these responses to the temporal judgments in two ways. An event selected during an object's temporal judgment receives additional support when the object's source is reported later. A remembered event ordering, based on global temporal context, influences temporal judgments throughout a round and is reported in the final event-order task.

During each judgment, positions consistent with this ordering receive additional support.

Retrieved context continues to contribute, so the temporal judgments need not agree with that ordering, and a later source report can differ from the earlier event assignment. These links are formalised as source-identity and event-order preferences in the Supplementary Information.

We therefore evaluate the joint probability of each round's temporal judgments and later reports in Experiment 2. The calculation averages over the event assignments and remembered orderings that could have produced those responses. Fitting thus constrains both the accuracy of the later reports and their relationship to the earlier judgments.

We maximized the likelihood using L-BFGS-B within specified parameter bounds (Byrd et al., 1995). For each experiment, we ran the optimizer from eight initial parameter sets and retained the solution with the highest likelihood. Parameter bounds, search settings, and numerical checks are reported under "Fitting and additional comparisons" in the Supplementary Information. Supplementary Table 3 reports the fitted parameter values.

Comparing data and simulations

We generated 200 complete datasets from each experiment's fitted model. Each simulated dataset preserves the experimental conditions and receives the same statistical analysis as the observed data. For Experiments 1, 3, and 4, Gaussian mixed-effects models estimate the condition means of participant-level order accuracy and distance ratings, with participant random intercepts. Experiment 2 uses logistic mixed-effects models for order accuracy and Gaussian mixed-effects models for distance. Its simulations generate the temporal judgments, source reports, and final ranking jointly; later-report categories are formed from those simulated reports.

Figures 8 and 9 show empirical estimates with one-standard-error bars and averaged model estimates without error bars.

For the additional numerical comparisons in Experiments 1 and 4, we averaged each participant's observations and exact model predictions, giving participants equal weight.

Empirical confidence intervals were obtained by resampling participants. Details appear under "Fitting and additional comparisons" in the Supplementary Information.

Model results and discussion

Figure 8 compares the main empirical effects with the fitted model across all four experiments. Within-event and cross-event test pairs had the same objective separations, with two or three intervening objects. The comparisons therefore concern differences in remembered temporal relationships at matched study separations.

Additional fits examined the contributions of positional evidence and the links between judgments and later reports by restricting these components of HCR. Comparisons across particular study positions and directions of retrieval errors provided further tests of the fitted account. Experiment 1: Effects of event reminders

Correct reminders improved order accuracy more for cross-event than within-event pairs, and the fitted model reproduces this difference. A reminder increases support for the object's studied event, making it more likely that the object retrieves temporal information from that event. This is especially useful across events, where a mistaken assignment can substitute the wrong event's position or assign both objects to one event. For a pair correctly assigned to one event, the shared event position cannot distinguish which object came first; their relative order depends on their positions within that event. Event identification therefore has different consequences for the two kinds of comparison.

RETRIEVAL AND EVENT SEGMENTATION 57

Reminders also lowered distance ratings for both types of pair, while cross-event pairs continued to seem farther apart. In the model, event assignment determines which event positions enter the objects' reconstructed separation. For an actual within-event pair, mistaken assignment to different events can introduce an unwarranted difference between event positions.

For an actual cross-event pair, substituting another event can place an object farther from its partner than their studied events would suggest. Correct reminders reduce these mistaken assignments. At the fitted values, the resulting distance reduction is larger for within-event pairs; cross-event pairs retain the separation between their two inferred events.

The assistance from correct reminders does not eliminate the within-event order advantage. With reminders present, that advantage is .054 in the data (95% CI [.027, .079]) and .034 in the model. The fit therefore preserves a cost of comparing two event positions even when the correct event identities are supplied. Experiment 1 supports an account in which useful event reminders improves temporal reconstruction while uncertainty in event position still limits crossevent order.

Experiment 2: Remembered sources and event order

Experiment 2 examined whether the event information associated with an earlier temporal judgment is also expressed in later reports. This tests more than overall order and distance performance: a model must account for which judgments accompany particular sourcememory and event-order reports. During model development, candidate accounts that reproduced the main patterns in Experiments 1, 3, and 4 failed to capture these relationships in Experiment 2. The proposed persistent preferences mechanism (see supplementary information) provides a link across these responses while allowing a later report to differ from the interpretation used earlier.

RETRIEVAL AND EVENT SEGMENTATION 58

In this experiment, both actual and reported event membership related to performance.

Objects studied within one event are ordered most accurately when later assigned to the same event. Objects studied in different events are ordered more accurately when later assigned to different events. Distance ratings were larger when the later reports name different events, but actual cross-event pairs also receive larger ratings than actual within-event pairs when both are reported as sharing an event. The model reproduces these broad relationships. Earlier event assignments influence later source reports and determine whether differences between event positions contribute to temporal reconstruction. The objects' local positional evidence and errors in later reporting allow actual study membership to matter within a reported-membership category.

The event-order reports provide a further distinction: identifying which events contained the objects does not ensure remembering those events in the right order. Figure 9 shows crossevent order accuracy by the number of correct source-memory reports and by whether the eventorder report places the objects' actual events in their correct relative order. Accurate later event order accompanies much higher temporal-order accuracy when both event identities are correct.

With only one correct identity, accuracy remains close to chance even when the order of the actual events is reported correctly. The model reproduces this conditional benefit. With both identities correct, its order accuracy is .764 for correct later event order and .471 for incorrect later order, compared with .774 and .474 observed. With one identity correct and correct later event order, it predicts .522, compared with .506 observed.

An event-order relation helps most when the objects are assigned to the events it relates.

For example, knowing that the art gallery preceded the café no longer supplies the relevant relation if the café's object is interpreted as belonging to the gift shop: the judgment now RETRIEVAL AND EVENT SEGMENTATION 59 compares the art gallery with the gift shop. Remembering the correct order of the art gallery and café can therefore coexist with a poor object-order judgment. In HCR, a remembered event ordering biases temporal judgments, while an event assigned during a judgment receives additional support in the later source report. The event retrieved for one object can also influence the event assigned to its partner. Errors arising this way can persist into later reports, affecting which judgments enter each report category. Experiment 2 therefore constrains both how event identity and order guide reconstruction and how the information used in a judgment remains related to later reports. Experiment 3: Changing event number and length

Experiment 3 tests the two levels of positional evidence by changing how a fixed-length sequence is divided into events. Longer events contain more local positions, while fewer events must be located in the full sequence. The model uses the same comparison rule at both levels, so a change in event structure must produce its effects through the contexts stored during study and the alternatives entering each comparison.

Order accuracy shows opposite event-membership advantages in the two schedules. With three long events, cross-event pairs are ordered more accurately than within-event pairs; with six short events, within-event pairs are more accurate. The model reproduces this reversal. Within a long event, the positional comparison must distinguish more candidates with more closely spaced reference values. Shorter events provide fewer and more separated reference values. At the global level, the three-event schedule provides fewer candidate event positions, and its longer events place successive events farther apart along the global context trajectory. Their overlap with sequence-beginning context therefore falls by a larger proportion between successive events, improving the discrimination of event positions at the fitted values. These differences allow the same comparison rule to favour cross-event or within-event pairs under the two schedules.

Distance ratings remain larger for cross-event than within-event pairs under both schedules, and the model reproduces that difference. Within one inferred event, only the difference in local positions contributes to separation. Across inferred events, their event positions also contribute. Uncertainty about the order of those events can leave a large estimated distance because the rating uses the magnitude of each possible separation. The global evidence can consequently support boundary expansion in distance even when it provides less reliable information about temporal order. The size of that expansion differs between schedules and is not fully captured by the model. These fits use one parameter set across both schedules, in which event number and event length changed together.

The component refits examined whether the reversal in order accuracy required information about positions at both levels. Making either local positions or event positions uninformative prevented the refitted model from reproducing the change from a cross-event advantage with three events to a within-event advantage with six events.

Additional comparisons across particular study positions identified further limits to the fitted account. These analyses provide more specific tests of the reconstruction than the aggregate boundary effects alone.

Experiment 4: Incorrect event reminders

Experiment 4 tests whether incorrect event reminders produces the kinds of temporal errors implied by reconstruction. If a reminder changes the event in which an object is placed, it can change both which object seems earlier and how far apart the objects seem. The direction of the error is therefore informative about how retrieved event and positional information enter the judgment.

Incorrect reminders impaired order accuracy and reversed the usual direction of the distance difference: within-event pairs seemed farther apart than cross-event pairs. The model captures both broad effects. An incorrect event reminders competes with remembered information about the object's event during identification. The inferred event then supplies global temporal context and gives greater weight to its objects when local position is reconstructed.

Treating the objects as belonging to different events introduces a possible difference between event positions, whereas treating them as belonging to one event removes that component. Errors in event assignment can consequently expand the distance of actual within-event pairs and compress the distance of actual cross-event pairs.

The particular wrong event reminders also matters. For actual cross-event pairs displayed with one common event reminder, order accuracy was .604 when that cue named the earlier event but .295 when it named the later event. The corresponding exact model predictions were .574 and .260. Assigning an object to the wrong event reduces its local support by favouring objects actually associated with that event. Because later positions have lower reference values, this reduction can shift the misassigned object towards a later position within the inferred event.

A common cue naming the earlier event can therefore make the later event's object seem later, favouring correct order. A common cue naming the later event can instead make the earlier object's reconstructed position later, favouring incorrect order. The model also captures the tendency to follow the displayed event order when it opposes the objects' actual order. These comparisons assess which temporal relation an incorrect reminder favours, alongside its effect on overall accuracy.

Experiment 4 connects the assistance from event reminders with the errors they can produce. The same retrieval operations that improve reconstruction when a display is accurate can favour a mistaken event assignment or temporal position when it is incorrect. The fit accounts for the direction of these effects, while the magnitude of the distance reversal remains a limitation.

General discussion

In four pre-registered experiments, we revisited two widely used behavioural markers of event segmentation: decreased temporal order memory accuracy and increased temporal distance ratings for pairs that span an event boundary compared to pairs that occur within the same event.

Although these effects are often interpreted as direct, mandatory consequences of event segmentation during encoding (Bangert et al., 2020; Clewett et al., 2020; Lohnas et al., 2023), our empirical results indicate that they depend strongly on retrieval processes, in particular, memory for item-event bindings, memory for the order of events, and reconstructive processes.

Our formal model, called Hierarchical Context Reconstruction, explained the empirical results as a shift to the balance of uncertain, noisy evidence during retrieval. As such, it offers a more comprehensive account than hitherto available of the retrieval processes that underly event cognition.

Experiment 1 was designed as a conceptual replication of Wen and Egner's Experiment 4 with greater ecological validity, implemented by using distinctive naturalistic events.

Surprisingly, we did not replicate their reported cross-boundary advantage in temporal order memory when event reminders were presented at test, instead observing the typical within-event advantage. The pattern of results suggested that better cross-boundary temporal order memory does not necessarily arise whenever reminders of distinctive events are present at test. It also suggested that source memory, namely memory for the event during which an item was encoded, contributes to temporal order and distance memory. Using a source-absent paradigm, where the event-defining source is not presented again during test, Experiment 2 showed that temporal order memory depended jointly on source memory and event-order memory. The results also provided the first evidence that temporal distance judgments were shaped by retrieval processes.

Experiment 3 varied the number and length of events, with fewer events expected to make event order easier to remember. Critically, with three longer events, temporal order memory was more accurate for cross-boundary than within-event pairs , a reversal of the usual pattern that was the 3-event than in the 6-event condition. HCR accounts for this difference with the same parameters in both conditions: fewer events leave fewer candidate event positions, while longer events allow temporal context to change further between successive events. This makes event order easier to reconstruct, improving cross-boundary item ordering because an item assigned to an earlier event is placed before an item assigned to a later event. Experiment 4 provided a causal test of the role of source information by experimentally manipulating whether the source information shown at test was correct or incorrect. Temporal order memory was higher when participants were cued with correct sources, showing that the fidelity of item-event information at retrieval has a causal influence on order judgments.

Accurately retrieving the source particularly benefited temporal order memory for crossboundary pairs compared to within-boundary pairs. In Experiment 1 reinstating source information at test selectively improved performance on cross-boundary trials and reduced the size of the within-event advantage, suggesting that cross-boundary pairs benefit more from source memory. This is because, as Wen and Egner also found (2022, Experiment 4) source memory is not sufficient to reverse the typical within-event advantage in temporal order memory. Experiment 2 showed that accurate event-order memory is also necessary. In experiment 2 item-event memory supported temporal order judgments only when participants also remembered the order of the relevant events. When event-order memory was incorrect, temporal order accuracy did not vary with source memory for the events in which items were encoded. When event-order memory was correct, accuracy was highest when participants remembered the source of both items. The error analysis in experiment 4 revealed that, on within-event trials with incorrect event reminders, incorrect temporal order judgments were biased toward the event order shown at test. This pattern suggests that participants often relied on incorrect source information, rather than on the encoded temporal order of the objects. These results suggest that accurate temporal judgments of cross-boundary pairs require a correct representation of the sequence of sources; when that sequence is misrepresented, reinstating the encoding source information provides limited support. This asymmetry suggests that the classic within-event advantage could be due not to event segmentation at encoding, but to the extra retrieval demands of cross-boundary judgments. Consequently, factors that affect the availability or use of source memory or event-order information at test -such as when there are many indistinct events, or when retrieval cues are absent or incorrect-can change the magnitude of classic "boundary effects," even without changes in segmentation at encoding. Our findings suggest that the "flipped" effect, first demonstrated by Wen and Egner (2022) and later by Ding and Zacks (2026), emerges when the retrieval conditions favour accurate event-order reconstruction.

Recent accounts of temporal order memory combine information about item position across the sequence and within events (Peng et al., 2025). They simulate the classic within-event advantage without modelling reliance on remembered event membership and event order. Our findings challenge these accounts to explain reversals of this advantage and the effects of event reminders available at retrieval.

Factors that govern temporal distance ratings

We were able to illuminate striking effects of retrieval processes on distance ratings because we used a different temporal distance measure compared to most prior work, which typically uses coarse ordinal scales [e.g., 4-point ratings such as very close, close, far, very far; Clewett et al. (2020); Ezzyat and Davachi (2014); J. Wang and Lapate (2025); Y. C. Wang and Egner (2022); Wen and Egner (2022)]. Here we used a 0-35 scale that matches the possible number of intervening items in our sequences, allowing direct comparison with the objective distance. This aspect of the methodology, recommended to us by the much respected, late Prof.

Sarah Dubrow, made it possible to observe two features of temporal distance judgments. First, in Experiment 1, temporal distance judgments were not sensitive to the objective number of intervening items. Second, across most experiments, subjective temporal distance ratings were substantially greater than the objective distances between tested items. Together, these results suggested that participants did not rely strongly on a fine-grained representation of temporal lag.

Instead, crossing an event boundary appeared to add about four additional items' worth of subjective temporal distance. Furthermore, they suggested that the boundary should not be simulated as a drift of the temporal context, as in previous accounts based on retrieved-context theory (Horner et al., 2016; Lohnas et al., 2023), since these accounts typically consider an event boundary to cause a drift of about the same magnitude of just one non-recallable item.

In Experiments 2, whenever participants believed that pairs were encoded in two separate events, and regardless of whether these events were encoded within or across boundary, they rated the pairs as farther apart than pairs judged as within-event. The importance of this belief is consistent with the result from Experiment 1 where elevated temporal distance ratings for objectively cross-boundary pairs emerged only when participants successfully remembered the encoding events of both test items. Experiment 4 provided direct causal evidence for this retrieval-based account. When incorrect event reminders made objectively within-event pairs appear cross-boundary, participants judged them as farther apart than with correct reminders.

Conversely, when incorrect event reminders made objectively cross-boundary pairs appear within-event, participants judged them as closer together than with correct reminders.

We deduced that temporal distance judgments are sensitive to reconstructed boundary representation, which can be biased by incorrect retrieval cues. Experiment 3 provided converging support: participants who studied three-event sequences tended to give higher distance ratings than those who studied six-event sequences, even when the objective lag between test pairs was matched, and even though event length did not alter temporal order accuracy. Together, these findings are difficult to explain as a direct consequence of encoding alone.

Overall, the pattern across Experiments 1-4 is consistent with an account of temporal distance ratings in which temporal distance judgments are downstream from reconstructed boundary structure. Believing that two items were encoded in separate events increases perceived distance, which is further stretched when these events have a longer duration.

Considering the structure of retrieved sequences when judging interval durations can be adaptive, but the ability of event reminders to modulate and even flip the effect of event segmentation on this measure challenges existing context-based accounts.

Theoretical implications

Contextual and hierarchical theories describe how events guide memory search (Farrell, 2012; Polyn et al., 2009). Related findings suggest that event information available at retrieval also contributes to temporal order judgments (Ding & Zacks, 2026; Wen & Egner, 2022). Our experiments show that this information can also distort temporal judgments: incorrect event reminders biased temporal order judgments and reversed the typical temporal distance effect, making objects studied within one event seem farther apart than objects studied across events.

Explaining both accurate and distorted temporal memory requires specifying how temporal information about individual objects is combined with source memory and event-order memory.

These links allow HCR to explain why correct event-membership reports accompany better cross-boundary ordering when event order is also reported correctly, and why pairs later assigned to different events are judged farther apart..

Accounting for these relationships advances the broader aim of connecting tasks within a common theory (Newell, 1990).

Further tests of HCR could distinguish the consequences of forgetting event order from those of remembering an object in the wrong event. People may remember that two objects came from different events but have to guess which came first. Even with this uncertainty, the objects can seem farther apart than objects remembered from the same event. Remembering the incorrect event can instead shift where an object is placed in time. An object mistakenly assigned to a later event should be judged later more often than one mistakenly assigned to an earlier event.

While HCR provided good fit of the key results of all four experiments, and therefore has potential to advance our understanding of event cognition, it does not currently encompass all known effects. Specifically, some effects of study position and the size of some distance effects remain poorly captured. Without comparison with alternative accounts, we cannot know whether HCR offers the best explanation. Future studies could vary the accuracy of event reminders while controlling the items' positions within events. Collecting event-membership and eventorder reports alongside temporal judgments would allow alternative accounts to be compared across all four responses.

Segmentation could aid later free recall even while errors in retrieving events distort pairwise temporal judgments. HCR does not predict which studied objects would be freely recalled, so it cannot explain that benefit. Neural reactivation at event offsets, reviewed by Silva et al. (2026), may help explain how event endings support memory formation.

In our experiments, manipulating event reminders changed temporal boundary effects while the studied sequence was held constant. Event-memory reports showed how temporal judgments varied with remembered event membership and order. Interpreting these effects as evidence of earlier segmentation therefore requires accounting for retrieval conditions. HCR takes the studied event structure as given, so its fit cannot tell us where a participant perceived boundaries. Independent reports of boundary perception at study, paired with temporal judgments under varied retrieval cues, could test when those judgments track perceived segmentation.

Conclusions

The effect of event boundaries on temporal memory are shaped by how participants reconstruct what they encoded, not only on the process of segmenting unfolding experience into separate events during encoding. Our empirical findings and simulations imply that widely studied, robust behavioural boundary effects in temporal memory should not be treated as markers of event segmentation at encoding. Instead, they are more likely to reflect a mixture of segmentation, associative encoding, the availability and use of source information at retrieval, and ecologically relevant heuristics about the nature and duration of events. Whenever those go awry, signatures of event segmentation is likely to be affected even when participants are perfectly able to perceive event boundaries, potentially explaining the link between poor segmentation ability and impaired functioning across several disorders.

Global context supplies evidence about an event's position in the sequence (event position), while local context supplies evidence about an object's position within its event (local position). Combining an event position with a local position gives the object's position among all objects in the sequence (sequence position). The reconstructed item positions provide a common basis for both judgments: order depends on which position is earlier, whereas distance depends on how far apart the positions lie. The model weights the possible reconstructions by their retrieved evidence to assign probabilities to order choices and distance ratings. Uncertainty about which of two events came first can therefore weaken an order judgment while preserving evidence that their objects occurred far apart. Experiment 4 showed that incorrect event reminders at retrieval reversed the usual distance effect, with within-event pairs judged farther apart than cross-boundary pairs. These results are consistent with a contribution of event-order memory to behavioural signatures of event segmentation.

This conclusion extends initial investigations by Wen and Egner (2022) and those of Ding and Zacks (2026). We provide data that support Wen and Egner's speculation that source retrieval is crucial, and specify the relative contributions of source memory and event order memory. Using narratives with meaningful hierarchical structure, Ding and Zacks (2026) showed that semantic knowledge about event order and hierarchical event organization can scaffold temporal order judgments and, in some cases, reverse the typical within-event advantage. These findings converge with ours in suggesting that temporal memory reflects the integration of multiple sources of information at retrieval, rather than a direct readout of event segmentation during encoding. We extend their results to situations where semantic knowledge is thinner, as in typical laboratory set-ups and many situations in real life. Furthermore, we show that the same conclusions apply to temporal distance ratings. Based on the results reported here and in these previous investigations, it is no longer possible to attribute behavioural "boundary effects" in temporal memory solely to segmentation processes at encoding.

Factors that govern the magnitude and direction of temporal order memory

In the four experiments, temporal order memory depended on the availability and fidelity of event-source information at retrieval and on the structure of the studied sequence, rather than only whether tested items had crossed an event boundary at encoding. In Experiment 1, crossboundary temporal order memory was better when source information was re-presented at test or endogenously retrieved. In Experiment 3, cross-boundary temporal order memory was higher in In the HCR model, each object's position in the sequence is reconstructed from evidence about its position within an event and that event's position in the sequence. Memory for event membership and any displayed event reminder guide the model's assignment of each object to an event. This assignment determines which event's temporal context is retrieved and which objects contribute more strongly to reconstructing the target object's position within that event.

Assigning an object to the wrong event can therefore distort both the reconstructed event position and the object's position within the event. The model uses the resulting positions to make both judgments: their relative order determines which object came first, while their separation determines temporal distance. This shared reconstruction process allows order and distance judgments to diverge. Objects assigned to different events can seem far apart even when the model is uncertain which event came first. The quantitative fits reproduce the two contrasting patterns in our experiments. With fewer, longer events, order memory is more accurate across than within events, while cross-boundary pairs are still judged as farther apart. With incorrect event reminders, cross-boundary pairs are judged as closer together than within-event pairs, while order memory remains more accurate within events. HCR thus explains how contrasting effects on order and distance judgments can arise from the same reconstructed positions, offering an account of how event information can support or distort temporal memory.

Experiments 1, 3, and 4 required HCR to capture classic and reversed effects of event boundary. Experiment 2 also required HCR to explain how these judgments relate to later reports of the objects' event membership and order. HCR links these responses by retaining event information across tests. The event used to locate an item remains favoured when its source is later reported. The item's learned event associations also influence that report, so an earlier error can persist or be corrected. The model also retains one remembered event ordering throughout hypothesized that participants' temporal distance judgments depend not only on what they encoded, but on what they retrieve, specifically whether they infer that the two items belonged to the same source (within-event) or to different sources (cross-boundary).

A natural prior, based on simple environmental statistics, is that items that were encoded in different sources were encoded far apart in time. If participants deploy such a heuristic, source memory accuracy could influence temporal distance ratings. Specifically, for pairs encoded in different sources, we predicted shorter distance ratings when participants incorrectly judged them as having been encoded in the same source. Conversely, for pairs encoded in the same source, we predicted larger distance ratings when participants incorrectly judged them as having been encoded in different sources.
